chunks: "The big pros of a sense resistor are that it's simple, cheap, small, and very linear.
It works from DC up to hundreds of kilohertz, there's no saturation or hysteresis, and with a good metal-strip part and a decent amplifier I can get well under one percent accuracy.
It also survives big overloads for short periods because it's just metal. The cons are mostly about the side effects.
It dissipates I to the 2R , and it drops voltage in the supply path, so it's a bad fit above roughly 50 to 100 amps.
The signal is tiny, so amplifier offset sets how small a current I can resolve. The resistance changes with temperature and self-heating, so accuracy drifts.
At fast switching edges its parasitic inductance adds an L dI over dt spike that corrupts the reading.
It has no isolation, and on the high side it sits at the bus voltage, so I need a CSA with enough common-mode range.
And layout matters: if I don't use a Kelvin connection, trace resistance becomes part of the measurement.
So I'd choose it for low to moderate currents without an isolation requirement, and go magnetic for isolation or very high current."
